visual.lectureScript:
This unit finishes the conditionals and then does something more useful than any of them.

The last conditional first. Unit 5 took the real ones. Unit 13 took the unreal present, and said so.
This one is the unreal past, and it is how English discusses a decision once the outcome is known.
If we had checked the log, the fault would have been found.
Both halves are about the past, and both are untrue. We did not check, and it was not found.
The shape is: past perfect in the if half, would have plus a participle in the other.
The rule you already know holds for the third time. No would in the if half, exactly as there was no will in Unit 5 and no would in Unit 13.
And one thing worth doing more often than most people do it.
Would have claims a great deal. It says the outcome was certain.
If we had checked, the fault MIGHT have been found is usually the honest version, because checking does not guarantee finding.

The second card sits right beside the first, because they describe the same moment from different angles.
Wish and if only, about the past, take the past perfect.
I wish we had checked the log. If only they had told us.
The regret and the consequence together make a complete account of a mistake, and most accounts give only one.
The error to watch is I wish I would have checked, which is very common and is not English.
Wish plus would is for other people's behaviour, and only in the present.

The third card extends Unit 13's past modals.
That unit gave you must have and can't have, for near certainty. Here are the weaker ones, and one pair that matters more than it looks.
We needn't have ordered more means we DID order them, and it was a waste.
We didn't need to order more means there was no need, so we probably did not.
Two sentences that sound almost identical, reporting opposite facts about whether the money was spent.
And could have is the mildest reproach English has. We could have asked. Nobody is blamed, and something is still being said.

Now the fourth card, which is the reason this unit exists.
Every argument has three parts and almost everybody states two.
There is the claim: the depot should close.
There is the evidence: its costs are twice the others'.
And there is the warrant, which is the link that lets the second support the first. Here, that cost should be what decides which depots close.
Nobody says the warrant. It does not need saying when everybody shares it.
Which means it goes unsaid exactly when it is not shared, which is exactly when it needs saying.
The reading in this unit is about four meetings spent arguing over figures that both sides had already agreed on.
They checked them, agreed, produced more, agreed again, and disagreed precisely as much as before.
One side thought cost should decide. The other thought access should. That is not a disagreement about evidence, and no evidence settles it.
There is a question that surfaces it every time, and it is worth memorising.
What would have to be true for this evidence to support that claim?
Ask it of your own arguments first. Yours have warrants too, and you cannot see them for the same reason the other side cannot see theirs.

The last card is a small set of adjectives that behave unlike any others you have met.
Sheer, utter, outright, mere, downright.
They go in front of a noun and they cannot go after the verb.
Utter nonsense is right. The nonsense was utter is not.
And notice what they do, because an argument reaches for them constantly.
A misrepresentation, against a total misrepresentation. The second is not more accurate. It is louder.
Use them where you can support the emphasis, and notice them when somebody uses them on you.

One last thing, from the consultation response in the reading.
It opens by conceding the figures entirely, which costs it nothing and removes them from the argument.
Then it names the unstated warrant. Then it makes its own case. Then it names two faults by their proper names: cherry-picking, and a strawman.
And it finishes by saying it would accept the outcome of a fair test whatever that outcome was.
That last sentence is what makes the whole thing hard to dismiss, and it is the only sentence in it that gives anything away.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: We Were Arguing About the Wrong Thing
readings.setting: After a long meeting about a depot
readings.passageScript:
We spent four meetings arguing about figures that everybody agreed on, and it took us until the fourth to notice.
The case for closing the northern depot was that its costs were twice the others'.
Nobody disputed the costs. Both sides had checked them, twice.
So we went round again, and produced more figures, and agreed about those too, and disagreed exactly as much as before.
What was actually in dispute was never said aloud by anybody.
One side thought cost was what should decide which depot closed. The other thought access was.
That is not a disagreement about evidence. No amount of evidence settles it.
Somebody finally said it in the fourth meeting, and the argument changed completely within about ten minutes.
Since then I have tried to ask one question early, and it saves a great deal of time.
What would have to be true for this evidence to support that claim?
If both sides answer it differently, more figures will not help.
If only we had asked it at the start, we would have had one meeting instead of four.
Granted, somebody has to be willing to say what they are assuming, and that is harder than it sounds.

readings.title: The Part of an Argument Nobody Writes Down
readings.passageScript:
An argument has three parts, and almost every argument states two of them.
There is the claim, which is what you want accepted.
There is the evidence, which is what you offer for it.
And there is the warrant, which is the link that lets the second support the first.
The depot should close. Its costs are twice the others'. Those are the claim and the evidence.
The warrant is that cost should decide which depots close, and nobody says it, because whoever is arguing thinks it is obvious.
That is exactly why it matters. A warrant only needs stating when it is not shared, and the moment it is not shared is the moment nobody states it.
This explains an experience most people have had.
Two sides check the figures, agree on the figures, and disagree just as much afterwards.
More evidence cannot settle a disagreement about a warrant, and producing it feels like progress while achieving nothing.
There is one question that surfaces the warrant every time.
What would have to be true for this evidence to support that claim?
Ask it of your own arguments before you ask it of anybody else's. Yours have warrants too, and you cannot see them for the same reason they cannot see theirs.

readings.title: Response to the Depot Consultation
readings.setting: A formal response to a closure proposal
readings.passageScript:
RESPONSE TO CONSULTATION: PROPOSED CLOSURE, NORTHERN DEPOT

1. What we accept
We concede that the operating costs of the northern depot are approximately twice
those of the other three. We have checked the figures and do not dispute them.

2. Where we disagree
The proposal assumes that operating cost should be the deciding criterion.
That assumption is not stated in the consultation, and it is the point at issue.
We would argue that access is the relevant criterion, for the reasons at 3 below.

3. Our case
The northern depot serves an area from which the other three are over an hour away.
If the northern depot had been closed in 2019 as previously proposed, the two
supply failures of that winter would have affected a further eleven sites.

4. Two objections to the proposal as argued
The comparison uses three months of data. A mere three months cannot establish a
pattern over a decade, and the months chosen were the depot's worst.
The proposal also states that we oppose all reorganisation. We do not, and we have
not said so. That is a strawman.

5. What we propose
That both criteria be stated, weighted, and applied to all four depots.
We would accept the outcome of that exercise whatever it showed.

grammar.title: The conditional that arrives too late
grammar.explanation:
This is the last conditional and it is new. Unit 5 took the real ones and
Unit 13 took the unreal present.
This one is about the past, and about something that did not happen. It is
how English discusses a decision after the outcome is known.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IF + past perfect, THEN would have + past participle.

If we had checked the log, the fault would have been found.
  (we did not check, and it was not found)
If they had told us, we would not have ordered more.
If the brake had been set, the trolley would not have moved.

Both halves are about the PAST, and both are untrue.
That is what separates it from the second conditional:
If we checked the log, the fault would be found.   (now, and we do not)
If we had checked, the fault would have been found. (then, and we did not)

COULD and MIGHT soften the second half:
If we had checked, the fault might have been found.
That is honest where would have claims too much.

MIXED, when the past cause still has a present effect:
If we had checked the log, we would not be here now.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Nobody checked the log and the fault was missed. Say it as a conditional.
1. Is it about the past? Yes, and both halves are untrue.
2. The if half takes the past perfect: if we had checked the log.
3. The other half takes would have plus a participle.
4. Ask whether would have claims too much. Would it certainly have been found?
Answer: If we had checked the log, the fault might have been found.
might have is the honest version unless you can show it certainly would have.
grammar.commonMistake:
would have never appears in the if half, exactly as will and would did not.
No: If we would have checked, the fault would have been found.
Yes: If we had checked, the fault would have been found.
One half carries would have, and it is not the half with if in it.
grammar.memoryTip: Past perfect in the if half. would have in the other. And prefer might have unless you are sure.
grammar.practice:
Write the third conditional.
1. We did not check the log. The fault was not found.
2. They did not tell us. We ordered more.
3. The brake was not set. The trolley moved.
4. Nobody asked. We did not know.
Now soften one of them with might have, and say why.
Now correct these.
5. If we would have checked, the fault would have been found.
6. If we had checked, the fault would be found.
grammar.answerKey:
1. If we had checked the log, the fault would have been found.
2. If they had told us, we would not have ordered more.
3. If the brake had been set, the trolley would not have moved.
4. If anybody had asked, we would have known.
Softening: number 1, because checking does not guarantee finding.
5. If we HAD checked.  6. ... would have been found. (both halves are past)
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: If only: the wish that arrives afterwards
grammar.explanation:
Unit 13 taught wish about the present. This is wish and if only about the
PAST, and it is the form regret actually takes.
It sits beside the card before it, because a third conditional and a past
wish describe the same moment from different angles.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
WISH or IF ONLY + past perfect:
I wish we had checked the log.
If only they had told us.
I wish I had not signed it.

IF ONLY is stronger than wish, and it is the one regret usually reaches for.

SET THEM SIDE BY SIDE with the conditional:
I wish we had checked the log.                    the regret
If we had checked, the fault would have been found. the consequence
The first says what you feel. The second says what would have followed.
A complete account of a mistake usually needs both.

AND FROM UNIT 13, THE PRESENT VERSIONS, for contrast:
I wish I knew.        a present fact
I wish I had known.   a past one
One word apart, and they are about different moments.

WISH + WOULD is still only for other people, and still only about behaviour:
I wish they would reply.  NOT: I wish I would have replied.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You signed something you should not have. Write the regret and the consequence.
1. The regret is about the past, so wish or if only plus the past perfect.
   I wish I had not signed it.
2. The consequence is a third conditional.
   If I had not signed it, we would not be liable.
Answer: both sentences, together.
Notice the second one is mixed: a past cause with a present effect.
grammar.commonMistake:
I wish I would have is not English, and it is very common.
No: I wish I would have checked.
Yes: I wish I had checked.
wish + would is for somebody else's behaviour, and only in the present.
grammar.memoryTip: wish or if only plus the past perfect. Never wish I would have.
grammar.practice:
Write the regret with wish or if only.
1. We did not check the log.
2. They did not tell us.
3. I signed it.
4. Nobody asked.
Now write the matching consequence as a third conditional for number 1.
Now answer.
5. What is the difference between I wish I knew and I wish I had known?
Now correct this.
6. I wish I would have checked.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I wish we had checked the log. / If only we had checked the log.
2. If only they had told us.  3. I wish I had not signed it.
4. If only somebody had asked.
Consequence: If we had checked the log, the fault would have been found.
5. The first is about a present fact; the second about a past one.
6. I wish I had checked.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: Needn't have, didn't need to
grammar.explanation:
Unit 13 gave you must have and can't have, for working out what was true.
Stage 9 adds the speculative ones, and one pair that learners never separate
because the two versions sound almost identical and describe different events.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
SPECULATION about the past, weaker than deduction:
It might have been the seal.   (possible; you do not know)
It could have been either.
They may well have known.
Compare Unit 13: it MUST have been the seal is near certainty.

THE PAIR, and this is the card:
We needn't have ordered more.   = we DID order more, and it was unnecessary.
We didn't need to order more.   = it was unnecessary, and we probably did not.
The first reports a wasted action. The second reports an absence of need.

COULD HAVE, for something possible that did not happen:
We could have asked. (we did not)
They could have told us at any point. (they did not)
This is the mildest reproach English has.

SHOULD HAVE, from Unit 13, is the strongest of the set.
So the ladder runs: could have, might have, needn't have, should have.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You ordered fifty more and it turned out there was plenty. Which one?
1. Did you order them? Yes.
2. Was it necessary? No.
3. An action you DID take, unnecessarily, is needn't have.
Answer: We needn't have ordered more.
We didn't need to order more would suggest you knew at the time, and did not.
grammar.commonMistake:
The two sound alike and report opposite facts about what you did.
We needn't have ordered more = the boxes are here, unopened.
We didn't need to order more = we did not order any.
In an account of a cost, that is the difference between wasted money and none.
grammar.memoryTip: needn't have = you did it and it was pointless. didn't need to = there was no need, so you probably did not.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right form.
1. We ordered fifty more; there was plenty. We ___ ordered more.
2. There was plenty, so we did not order any. We ___ order more.
3. It is possible it was the seal; you do not know. It ___ the seal.
4. Nothing else touches that line; you are nearly certain. It ___ the seal.
5. Asking was possible and we did not. We ___ asked.
6. It was our duty and we failed. We ___ asked.
Now answer.
7. Put could have, might have, needn't have and should have in order of strength.
grammar.answerKey:
1. needn't have  2. didn't need to  3. might have been  4. must have been
5. could have  6. should have
7. could have, might have, needn't have, should have.
1 and 2 report opposite facts about whether the order was placed.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Claim, evidence, warrant: the part nobody writes down
grammar.explanation:
Every argument has three parts and almost everybody writes two.
The missing one is where disagreements actually live, and learning to see it
is worth more than any amount of persuasive vocabulary.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE THREE PARTS:
CLAIM     what you want accepted.   The depot should close.
EVIDENCE  what you offer for it.    Its costs are twice the others'.
WARRANT   the link that joins them. Cost should decide closures.

The warrant is almost never stated. It does not need to be when everybody
shares it — and it needs to be when they do not.

Most real disagreement is about the warrant, not the evidence.
Both sides may accept the costs. One thinks cost should decide; the other
thinks access should. Arguing harder about figures will not settle that.

SO THE MOVE IS: state the warrant out loud.
'I am assuming cost should decide. If you think access matters more, that is
the disagreement, and figures will not settle it.'

THE FOUR PLACES AN ARGUMENT BREAKS:
thin or cherry-picked evidence
an unshared, unstated warrant
a claim bigger than the evidence supports
circular reasoning, or a strawman
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Somebody argues: the depot should close, because its costs are twice the others'.
Find the warrant.
1. What is the claim? The depot should close.
2. What is the evidence? Costs are twice the others'.
3. What must be true for the second to support the first?
4. That cost is what should decide which depots close.
Answer: the warrant is that cost should be the deciding criterion.
Nobody said that, and it is the only part worth arguing about.
grammar.commonMistake:
Arguing about evidence when you disagree about the warrant never ends.
Both sides check the figures again, agree on them, and disagree exactly as
much as before.
If more evidence is not moving anybody, the disagreement is a warrant.
grammar.memoryTip: Claim, evidence, warrant. The warrant is unstated, and it is what you actually disagree about.
grammar.practice:
For each argument, name the claim, the evidence and the warrant.
1. The depot should close; its costs are twice the others'.
2. She should get the post; she has eleven years on site.
3. The clause is unfair; nobody reads it before signing.
4. The figures are wrong; they contradict last year's.
Now answer.
5. In number 2, what would somebody who disagreed most likely be disputing?
6. Name the four places an argument breaks.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Claim: close it. Evidence: costs. Warrant: cost should decide.
2. Claim: she should get it. Evidence: eleven years. Warrant: length of service
   should decide, or at least count heavily.
3. Claim: unfair. Evidence: nobody reads it. Warrant: a term nobody reads
   cannot fairly bind them.
4. Claim: wrong. Evidence: contradiction. Warrant: last year's figures are right.
5. The warrant. They probably accept the eleven years and deny it should decide.
6. Thin or cherry-picked evidence; an unshared warrant; a claim too big for the
   evidence; circular reasoning or a strawman.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: Sheer, outright, downright: the adjectives that only go in front
grammar.explanation:
Unit 2 built compound and participle adjectives, and Unit 14 put a size on a
comparison. This is the last adjective card in the course, and it covers a
small set that behaves unlike every other adjective you have met.
They intensify a noun, and they cannot go after the verb.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
sheer      the sheer scale of it      NOT: the scale was sheer
utter      utter nonsense             NOT: the nonsense was utter
outright   an outright refusal        NOT: the refusal was outright
downright  downright dishonest        (this one CAN precede an adjective)
complete   a complete failure
total      a total misrepresentation
mere       a mere three cases

These are ATTRIBUTIVE ONLY: before the noun and nowhere else.
An ordinary adjective goes in both places:
a serious failure / the failure was serious.
an utter failure / the failure was utter — the second does not work.

WHAT THEY DO IN AN ARGUMENT: raise the temperature, add nothing checkable.
a misrepresentation / a total misrepresentation
The second is not more accurate. It is louder.
Use them where you can support the emphasis, and notice them when they are
used on you.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say a refusal was total and final. Which word, and where?
1. outright carries total and final.
2. It is attributive only, so it must precede the noun.
3. an outright refusal.
Answer: They gave an outright refusal.
The refusal was outright is what learners write, and it does not work,
because outright cannot follow the verb.
grammar.commonMistake:
These cannot go after be, however natural it feels.
No: The nonsense was utter. The scale was sheer.
Yes: utter nonsense. The sheer scale of it.
If you need it after the verb, choose an ordinary adjective: the refusal was flat.
grammar.memoryTip: Before the noun only. And they add emphasis, not evidence.
grammar.practice:
Put each one in a correct sentence.
1. sheer  2. utter  3. outright  4. mere
Now correct these.
5. The nonsense was utter.
6. The refusal was outright.
7. The scale was sheer.
Now answer.
8. What does 'a total misrepresentation' add over 'a misrepresentation'?
grammar.answerKey:
1. The sheer scale of it surprised everybody.
2. That is utter nonsense.
3. They gave an outright refusal.
4. It rests on a mere three cases.
5. That is utter nonsense.  6. It was an outright refusal.
7. The sheer scale of it was surprising.
8. Emphasis, and nothing checkable. It is not more accurate, only stronger.
6 or more right: good.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Six regrets and their consequences
writing.promptAndInstructions:

as a third conditional.

assignments.title: The response that is hard to dismiss
assignments.instructions:
Part one. Take a proposal you disagree with, real or invented, and write its
three parts as its author would: the claim, the evidence, and the warrant they
did not state.
Part two. Write a formal response in five sections, about 180 words:
what you accept, where you disagree, your case, objections to how it was argued,
and what you propose.
Section 1 must concede something that costs you. Section 2 must name their warrant.
Section 3 must contain one third conditional. Section 4 must name two faults from
group 4 and show the evidence for each naming.
Section 5 must offer a test whose outcome you would accept either way.
Part three. Write four sentences of regret using wish or if only, about how the
situation reached this point, and one matching third conditional.
Part four. Now state YOUR own warrant — the assumption behind your own case —
and one sentence on what would change your mind.
